lead: At first sight the readings seem to be about small practical things: how to save money for a collection, and what may be done on a sabbath. In both, the Lord's day and mercy come together. Paul asks the Corinthians to set money aside for the poor “on the first day of every week”. Jesus defends his hungry disciples with the word of Hosea, “I desire mercy”.

set: Paul is ending his letter from Ephesus (16:8). One of the great projects of his life was a collection among his Gentile churches for the poor among the believers in Jerusalem (Romans 15:25–28; 2 Corinthians 8–9; Galatians 2:10). It was relief for the hungry, and also a visible sign that Jew and Gentile were one Church in Christ.
str: v. 1: the same directions as for the churches of Galatia.
v. 2: the method: every week, each person, according to what he can save.
vv. 3–4: trustworthy carriers, approved by the church.
kw: A rare word in the New Testament, found only here (vv. 1–2). Elsewhere Paul prefers richer religious words for the same collection: fellowship, service, grace.
the first day of the week
The day of the Lord's resurrection (Mark 16:2; Acts 20:7). This verse is one of the earliest signs that Christians gave a special place to this day of the week.
In v. 3 the word for “your gift” is simply “grace”. The money is a grace that passes from God, through them, to the poor.
vv: On the first day of every week, each of you is to put aside and save whatever extra you earn, so that collections need not be taken when I come.
Regular and small, planned and not emotional. Each one gives; nobody is left out. Paul does not want people pressured at the last moment.
And when I arrive, I will send any whom you approve with letters to take your gift to Jerusalem.
Paul handles money with care. The church itself chooses the carriers and he gives them letters. Honesty in Church money is an old apostolic concern.
ch: The Catechism cites this passage when it says that from the very beginning Christians brought, along with the bread and wine for the Eucharist, gifts to share with those in need (CCC 1351). About a century after Paul, St Justin Martyr describes how the Sunday assembly collected gifts to help orphans, widows, the sick, prisoners and strangers (First Apology 67). Sunday worship and care for the poor have always gone together (CCC 2178, 2443–2449).

r.h: The Son of Man is lord of the sabbath
set: Just before this passage Jesus has said, “Come to me, all you that are weary… and I will give you rest” (11:28). Now the question of rest arises in practice. To pluck grain by hand from a neighbour's field was allowed (Deuteronomy 23:25). The objection is that it was done on the sabbath, when reaping was forbidden (Exodus 34:21). The Pharisees were not being petty: they were serious about guarding a holy day, which was God's gift and a sign of Israel's covenant. Such debates about what the sabbath allows were common among Jewish teachers of the time.
str: vv. 1–2: the disciples are hungry; the Pharisees object.
vv. 3–4: first argument: David and the bread of the Presence (1 Samuel 21:1–6).
vv. 5–6: second argument: priests work in the Temple on the sabbath (Numbers 28:9–10); “something greater than the temple is here”.
v. 8: the claim: the Son of Man is lord of the sabbath.
kw: In Hosea 6:6 this stands for the Hebrew ḥesed, loyal love. Matthew alone has Jesus quote this verse, and he does so twice (9:13; 12:7).
The word is neuter, “something greater”. It can point to Jesus' own person, or to the Kingdom present in him. Either way, a claim of this size goes far beyond an argument about grain.
vv: I tell you, something greater than the temple is here.
If Temple service permits work on the sabbath, how much more does service to the one who is greater than the Temple?
But if you had known what this means, ‘I desire mercy and not sacrifice,’ you would not have condemned the guiltless.
Hosea does not reject sacrifice. It is a Hebrew way of saying “this first, and that only with it”. Worship without mercy is empty.
For the Son of Man is lord of the sabbath.
Jesus claims the authority of the one who gave the sabbath. He does not abolish the day. He teaches its true meaning.
ch: The Catechism says that Jesus never failed to respect the holiness of the sabbath, and gave its law its authentic and authoritative interpretation (CCC 2173). It also cautions against the idea that Jesus simply opposed the Pharisees: his relations with them were not only polemical, and he had much in common with them (CCC 575–576, 579). It uses the same word of Hosea to teach that outward sacrifice must express the heart (CCC 2100). The Christian Sunday keeps this spirit: it is a day for God, for rest, and for works of mercy (CCC 2185–2186).

qa: Do Christians have to keep the sabbath?

The Christian keeps the Lord's Day, Sunday, the day of the Resurrection, which fulfils the spiritual truth of the sabbath (CCC 2175–2176). The commandment remains, and it is lived on the day of the new creation.
study: Paul asks for a small, regular amount set aside weekly. What would it mean for my family to plan our giving in this way?
Where might I be defending a rule while forgetting the person who is hungry?
